## What We Did

Reviewed Poisson models and introduced logistic regression, using recidivism as a case study.

## Key Concepts


#### Odds vs Probability

- Probability: percent chance of happening
- Odds: P/(1-P)
  - "How many more times is a specific outcome likely to happen again"
  - The probability something will happen divided by the probability that it will not happen
- Ex: If probability = 80%, then the odds = 4
- Ex: If probability = 50%, then the odds = 1 (i.e. even odds)
- Ex: If probability = 45%, then the odds = 0.835
  - Could be interpreted as: For every 100 people not sick with the flu, 84 are 
- Convert probability into log-odds to be able to use GLM
- Interpretation: Log-odds > 0 means odds-ratio > 1, which means probability > 50% (i.e. more likely than not)
  - (Odds − 1) × 100 = percent change in the odds
  - If log-odds are 0.16, then the odds-ratio is 1.17, which means that the odds increased by 17%
  

|Probability| Odds | Log-Odds |
| --- | :---: | ---: |
| 0.01| 0.01  | -4.6 |
| 0.10| 0.11  | -2.2 |
| 0.50| 1     | 0    |
| 0.80| 4     | 1.4  |
| 0.90| 9     | 2.2  |
| 0.99| 99    | 4.6  |
| 0-1 | 0 - ∞ | -∞ - +∞| 

*Log-odds in this case is natural log


#### Generalized Linear Modeling (GLM)

- Using a linear combination of variables
- Applies to both Poisson and logistic regression
- Link (g): maps outcome to predictors without breaking the boundary rules
- Inverse Link (g^-1): maps predictors to the outcome; turns a mathematical score into "real-world" prediction

|Model| Random Component | Bounded Expected Values | Link Function | Inverse Link |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | ---: |
| Logistic | Binomial | Probability P(0,1) | Logit Link ln(P/(P-1)) | g^-1 |
| Poisson  | Poisson  | (0, infinity)  | Log Link log(mu)  | Sigmoid Function (e^n) / (1+e^n) |

*Sigmoid = "S-curve"

#### Probability (P): P = (e^z)/(1 + e^z) where z = B_0 + B_1 x_1 + ...

- If z > 0, then p > 50% 
- If z < 0, then p < 50%
- If z = 0, then there is exactly 50% risk


#### Criminal Risk Assessment Algorithms

- Ex: COMPAS 
  - Uses 137 question survey as input data
  - Takes into account criminal history, history of violence, family history, mental health and personality traits, attitudes about the legal system
- U.S. Supreme Court failed to hear case about use of COMPAS in determining a person's sentencing
- Researchers have found that COMPAS was about as accurate as very simple or random predictive models
- COMPAS has since updated their model


#### Geographic Cross-Validation

- K-fold cross-validation imperfect for spatial data
  - Spatial autocorrelation causes spatial leakage (which makes the model seem like it's performing better than it actually does)
- In the case of using a fishnet grid as the spatial units, better to divvy up the cells into districts rather than use random k-folds


#### Logistic Regression

- For predicting binary outcomes (yes/no, etc.)
- Model: log(P/(1-P)) = B0 + B1x1 + B2x2 + ...
- Code: glm(y ~ x, family = binomial, data = dataset)
- Choose a threshold probability to determine what counts as "yes" and what counts as "no"
  - Ex: all probabilities over 50% are coded as "yes"

|Prediction| Actual 1 | Actual 0 |
| --- | :---: | ---: |
| 1| True Positive  | False Positive |
| 0| False Negative | True Negative  |

False positives and false negatives are inversely correlated (when one decreases, the other increases)


#### Specificity vs Sensitivity

- Sensitivity: Of all the observations that were actually 1, how many did the model accurately predict?
  - Calculation: True Positive / (True Positive + False Negative)
- Specificity: Of all the observations that were actually 0, how many did the model accurately predict?
  - Calculation: True Negative / (True Negative + False Positive) 
- Precision: Of all the observations that were predicted to be 1, how many did the model accurately catch?
  - Calculation: True Positive / (True Positive + True Negative)
- Accuracy: How accurately did the model predict true positives and negatives?
